what_its_for: This medication is a combination hormonal birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (levonorgestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the lining of the uterus. It may also be prescribed to regulate menstrual cycles, reduce cramps, or treat acne in some cases.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Try to pick a time that is easy for you to remember, such as with breakfast or before bed. Swallow the pill whole with or without food. If you feel nauseous, taking it with food or at bedtime may help. Follow the pills in the pack in the exact order shown — do not skip pills or take them out of order. When you finish one pack, start the next pack the very next day unless your pack includes reminder (inactive/placebo) pills — take those as directed too.
dosing: The usual dose is one active hormone pill taken once daily for 21 days followed by 7 reminder (inactive/sugar) pills, OR in extended-cycle packs, one active pill daily for 84 days followed by 7 inactive or low-dose estrogen pills. Your specific pack and schedule will depend on the brand your doctor prescribed. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's specific instructions for your pack.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue your regular schedule. You likely do not need a backup method. If you miss 2 or more pills in a row: Take the most recently missed pill right away and throw away the other missed pills. Continue taking the rest of your pack on schedule. Use a backup birth control method (such as condoms) for the next 7 days. If you missed pills in the third week of your pack or missed 3 or more pills, contact your pharmacist or doctor for guidance. If you had unprotected sex during the time you missed pills, talk to your doctor about emergency contraception. When in doubt, use a backup method and call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills past the expiration date printed on the pack. Dispose of unused or expired medication properly — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking cigarettes, especially if you are 35 years of age or older, as smoking combined with estrogen-containing pills significantly increases your risk of serious blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may affect how your body processes this medication. Avoid taking this pill with certain medications without telling your doctor, including rifampin (an antibiotic), seizure medications (such as phenytoin or carbamazepine), HIV medications, St. John's Wort, and some antifungals, as these can make your birth control less effective. Avoid prolonged bed rest or long periods of immobility (such as long flights), as this may increase your risk of blood clots.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following warning signs — use the word ACHES to remember: A — Abdominal pain (severe stomach pain); C — Chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood; H — Headaches that are severe or sudden; E — Eye problems such as blurred vision, loss of vision, or seeing flashing lights; S — Severe leg pain or swelling in the calf or thigh. Also contact your doctor if you notice: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), unusual or heavy vaginal bleeding, a lump in your breast, symptoms of depression such as feeling very sad or having mood changes, signs of an allergic reaction (rash, hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat), or if you have not had a period and think you may be pregnant.
when_it_works: If you start this pill on the first day of your period (Day 1 start), you are protected against pregnancy right away. If you start on any other day (such as the first Sunday after your period begins — a Sunday start), you will need to use a backup method of birth control such as condoms for the first 7 days of taking the pill. It may take 1 to 3 months for your periods to become regular and for you to adjust to the hormones. Some side effects like nausea or spotting between periods (breakthrough bleeding) often improve after the first 2 to 3 months.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking this pill, stop taking it and call your doctor right away. Breastfeeding: Estrogen-containing pills may reduce your milk supply. Talk to your doctor before using this medication if you are breastfeeding. A progestin-only pill ('mini-pill') may be a safer option while nursing. Teenagers: This medication is safe for teenagers who have already started their menstrual periods. Older adults/Women over 35: Women who smoke and are over 35 should NOT use this medication due to a significantly higher risk of serious cardiovascular side effects. Women over 35 who do not smoke should discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor. Liver disease: This medication should not be used by people with active liver disease or a history of liver tumors. Blood clot history: Tell your doctor if you or a close family member has ever had blood clots, as this may affect whether this medication is safe for you. Migraines with aura: Women who experience migraines with aura (visual disturbances before a headache) should not use estrogen-containing pills due to increased stroke risk.
